title: Young people experience digital life as both community infrastructure and an inescapable system of platform control, surveillance and harm
source_unit: Nuffield Foundation and Ada Lovelace Institute, I love it, but I hate it: Young people's experiences and expectations of growing up digital
geography: United Kingdom; peer research across Dundee, Shetland, Islington and Sandwell, spanning rural, urban and suburban contexts

observations.period: 2025–2026 research; young people aged 14–24 in four UK locations

denominator.unit: young people participating in peer research; purposive qualitative cohort

digital_connection.value: Participants described digital connection as an important route to information, advice, entertainment, community and relationships

marginalised_support.value: For some marginalised young people, online spaces provide comfort and support not readily available in their immediate offline environment

online_harm.value: Participants also described exposure to sexual, violent, hateful, discriminatory and misinformation content, including experiences that felt inescapable and difficult to challenge

observations.method: Peer research co-designed and facilitated by young people with youth-worker support; participants included people experiencing poverty, homelessness or social care, school exclusion, and health challenges.
observations.uncertainty: The cohort was purposive and qualitative; shared themes indicate lived experience and perceived mechanisms, not prevalence, representative population exposure or causal mental-health effects.
observations.subgroup: Young people aged 14–24 across four UK locations, with attention to gender, trans identity, care experience, exclusion and marginalization.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital communities can reduce isolation and expand support while still exposing people to harm; a single overall judgment that technology is beneficial or harmful would erase this context dependence.

observations.period: 2025–2026 research; digital-first everyday life and platform control

denominator.unit: young people participating in peer research; purposive qualitative cohort

digital_first_dependency.value: Participants said smartphones and digital technologies are integrated into essential tasks including schoolwork, paid-work applications and public services

control_constraint.value: They described being advised to reduce use while simultaneously being required to participate in a digital-first society, limiting control over when and how they go online

platform_design.value: Algorithmic nudges, gamification and dark patterns were understood as shaping attention and promoting commercial or ideological content

observations.method: Peer-led workshops and co-analysis focused on participants' own experiences of social media, messaging, search, schoolwork, work applications and AI.
observations.uncertainty: Participants' accounts identify perceived dependence and design mechanisms but do not measure screen time, algorithmic exposure, platform revenue effects or the prevalence of particular design experiences.
observations.subgroup: Young people navigating school, work, public services and relationships through digital systems, including those with limited offline support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital dependence may reflect useful access and convenience as well as coercive infrastructure; reducing use without providing offline alternatives could increase exclusion.

denominator.unit: young people participating in peer research; purposive qualitative cohort

self_safeguarding.value: Participants described having to independently manage online safety, with young women and trans participants especially reporting responsibility for themselves and younger people

structural_accountability.value: The perceived absence of structural accountability for harmful content and negative outcomes intensified isolation and resignation

surveillance_anxiety.value: Participants associated constant digital surveillance with anxiety and warned that safety measures could increase data collection and privacy loss

observations.method: Youth-led discussion and reflection, including attention to gendered experiences, past exposure and changing interpretation over time.
observations.uncertainty: The report records participant perceptions and narratives; it does not independently verify platform practices, legal harms, clinical diagnoses or differential exposure rates.
observations.subgroup: Young women, trans participants, younger children reflected on by older participants, and young people with varied care, health and exclusion experiences.
observations.counterinterpretation: Individual safety strategies and critical awareness can provide agency, but placing the burden on young people may conceal the responsibilities of platforms, regulators, schools, families and public services.

observations.period: 2025–2026 research; AI, future work and youth governance preferences

denominator.unit: young people participating in peer research; purposive qualitative cohort

ai_systemic_concerns.value: Participants raised concerns about AI's effects on arts, environment, sex and relationships, mental health, jobs, deskilling and public services

future_protection.value: Participants broadly wanted future young people to have stronger protections and not access technology in the same way they had, while preserving beneficial community access

youth_governance.value: The report recommends a standing, diverse Young People's Board on Digital Futures with representation, scrutiny, monitoring, deliberation and accountability functions

regulatory_balance.value: Age-specific protections should be combined with safety-by-design, privacy safeguards, broader platform regulation and investment in alternative digital and physical spaces

observations.method: Peer research synthesis and policy implications developed by the Ada Lovelace Institute from participants' lived experiences and reflections.
observations.uncertainty: The recommendations are normative and grounded in a small qualitative cohort; the report does not evaluate a youth board, regulation, safety-by-design intervention or alternative-space investment.
observations.subgroup: Young people affected by platform design, AI, public-service digitization, school technology and online/offline community access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Youth participation can improve policy fit and legitimacy, but a standing board requires clear power, representation, resources, feedback and accountability or it may become symbolic consultation.

related_sources.claim: Official Nuffield Foundation landing page with executive summary, participant context and policy implications.
Programme context for the Youth Insight Group, youth-worker partnership and broader journeys-to-adulthood research.

boundary: This record adds a UK comparative lived-experience layer: digital connection is simultaneously community infrastructure and an inescapable system of platform control, surveillance, harm and unequal exposure. It is peer-led qualitative research with 49 young people, not a prevalence survey, representative estimate, behavioral trace, clinical assessment, legal finding or causal evaluation of regulation, platform design or youth governance.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official 116-page Nuffield Foundation/Ada Lovelace Institute PDF and publication page were retrieved and reviewed for participant count, locations, peer-research design, digital benefits and harms, platform dependence, surveillance, AI concerns, subgroup context and policy implications; the PDF was hashed.
